cultivar: Small- and medium-leaf cultivars, including Baiye 1, Huangjinya and local population plants
processing: Young shoots are lightly spread to cool, fixed at high temperature, straightened and shaped, then pan-dried to lift the aroma.
harvest_season: Spring; the main picking falls in late March and early April.
appearance_dry: Long, slim, bright green strands, compared to new willow shoots.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright, a pale green-yellow.
taste_profile: An elegant, high aroma and a fresh, mellow taste.

brewing.notes: These are usual settings for a slim spring green. A glass lets you watch the strands, and cooler water protects the sweetness.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest, with picking concentrated in late March and early April. As with other Jiangsu greens, it is best within a year and is not aged.
description:
Lüyang Chun is a modern green tea from the low hills west of Yangzhou, with Yizheng and its Nashan area at the centre. The name means green-willow spring, and the long slim leaf really does look like a new willow shoot.

It is made from tender shoots that are cooled briefly, fixed at high heat, straightened and pan-dried. A local study comparing five cultivars grown in Yizheng found Baiye 1 best suited to this style, ahead of population plants and Huangjinya, and Fuding Dahao clearly weaker in aroma and taste. So the plant behind your bag matters.

The cup is clear and fresh, with a refined aroma and a mellow finish. Treat it gently: water around 80 °C and an open vessel, as with other slim spring greens.

It is mostly a regional tea. Check for the Yizheng origin and the year, and buy the freshest spring lot you can.
history:
Lüyang Chun dates from 1991, so it is young, though it draws on an older local story: tea from the Yangzhou area is traced to the Tang and Song, and the Shugang hills on the edge of the city gave their name to a tea offered as tribute under the Song.

Over the following three decades the tea picked up awards at provincial and national competitions, and a group standard now describes how reference samples are made. Older plantings from the 1990s survive around Nashan.
